proxy_language: Dogon (Dogon language cluster, esp. Toro So / Donno So / Tommo So of the Bandiagara Escarpment, Mali)
proxy_rationale: The name 'Cliff-and-Mask' evokes the Bandiagara Escarpment cliff settlements and the Dama/Sigi mask societies of the Dogon, so Dogon is the most defensible attested language for the region and imagery. Dogon is a Dogon-family language of uncertain Niger-Congo affiliation (Glottolog lists Dogon as an independent family). The link between a game 'court' and any real Dogon polity is loose, hence low confidence. Current game strings such as 'ye semas' are not Dogon-like and are not used as models.
phonology: Tommo So-type system (Heath 2008; McPherson 2013): consonants p b t d c j k g (kp gb marginal), m n ny ng, f s h, l r w y, plus implosive-free plain stops. Vowels: 7 vowel qualities i e E a O o u (often written i e \u025b a \u0254 o u), with phonemic length (long vowels written doubled) and ATR contrasts in some varieties. Lexical tone (high/low, with tone melodies on stems) is significant but normally unwritten in practical orthography. Nasal vowels occur in some varieties.
phonotactics: Native roots are typically CV(C), CVCV, CVCVC, CVVC; most stems 1-3 syllables. Syllable-final consonants limited mainly to nasals, l, r, sometimes y/w; no word-initial consonant clusters; no native complex codas. Words end in vowels or a sonorant; voiceless obstruents are rare finally. Consonant-vowel alternation is strict; clusters occur only as nasal + stop across syllable boundary (mb, nd, ng, nj).
orthography: Practical Latin transliteration as in Mali's national alphabet: p b t d c j k g m n ny ng f s h l r w y; vowels a e i o u plus \u025b \u0254 (or e/o with diacritics); long vowels doubled (aa, ee, oo); nasalization by tilde or following n in some systems; tone omitted. Names are written as separate words, capitalized; compound names are often written as one word or hyphenated.
morphology: Agglutinating, head-final (SOV). Nouns have no noun classes or gender; plural by suffixes (-n\u025b / -ye / -mO depending on variety), definiteness by enclitics, case-like postpositions. Verbs take suffixes for aspect, negation, and derivation (causative, reflexive, reciprocal); stems often end in vowel. Derivational suffixes make agent nouns (-ma, -mo) and abstract nouns.
compounding: Genitive constructions are juxtaposition of possessor then possessed (Y X = 'Y's X'), with tonal rather than segmental marking; relational postpositions follow the noun. Agent nouns: object + verb stem + agentive suffix ('X-maker'). Place names often noun + locative or descriptive stem (e.g., 'rock/cliff' + noun). Compounds are head-final: the modified noun comes last.
noun_phrase_order: Possessor before possessed; noun before adjective in some constructions but modifier-before-head in genitive; demonstratives and numerals follow the noun; plural/definite markers are phrase-final enclitics.

sources: Heath, Jeffrey. A Grammar of Jamsay (2008)
Heath, Jeffrey. A Grammar of Toro So / Tommo So Dogon (2018)
McPherson, Laura. A Grammar of Tommo So (2013)
Calame-Griaule, Genevi\u00e8ve. Ethnologie et langage: la parole chez les Dogon (1965)
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. The culture is geographically broad (Sahel, Sahara, central African forests), so Dogon is only a Sahelian proxy; forest or Saharan elements would need other proxies (e.g., Bantu or Songhay) and are not covered here. Some glosses and forms are given from Dogon ethnographic literature; real forms vary by Dogon variety and should be verified against Heath/McPherson before reuse.
